content: Fourth-generation assays are generally unable to distinguish between prior exposure to hepatitis C virus (HCV) and chronic HCV infection. This limitation is particularly relevant in individuals who are co-infected with HIV. There is insufficient data from systematic reviews to formally evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for detecting HCV antibodies in HIV/HCV co-infected individuals. In HIV-positive individuals, those undergoing immunosuppressive therapy or renal dialysis may not exhibit detectable HCV exposure, with this phenomenon estimated to occur in up to 6% of HIV-infected individuals tested using enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) for HCV antibodies. This issue is more pronounced in individuals with advanced immunosuppression due to HIV or during the early stages of HCV infection. Conversely, false-positive HCV serological test results are frequently reported among HIV-infected individuals, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. The Guidelines Development Group decided against defining minimum performance criteria for assays but recommended that any assay used should meet the performance standards set by stringent regulatory authorities. Certain RDTs are not validated for use with capillary whole blood, and issues related to analytical sensitivity and limit of detection (LoD) for HCV antibody assays are less critical compared to hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) detection. This is because there are no WHO reference standards for anti-HCV antibodies, and the differences in endpoint titers between RDTs and EIAs for HCV antibodies are minimal. The group conditionally recommended a one-assay serological testing strategy using either an RDT or EIA, followed by HCV RNA nucleic acid testing (NAT) or core antigen testing for reactive specimens. This approach is considered the simplest and most feasible testing strategy across various settings, based on low-quality evidence. Predictive modeling suggests that a single-assay strategy effectively identifies nearly all individuals likely to be infected and in need of NAT testing to confirm viremia, while excluding nearly all uninfected individuals, even in low-prevalence populations. The addition of a second assay has a smaller impact on improving positive predictive value (PPV) compared to HBsAg testing due to the generally higher sensitivity and specificity of RDTs for HCV antibodies. Concerns about the cost and feasibility of implementing a second serological assay, particularly in resource-limited settings, were noted. In low-prevalence populations, a higher proportion of false-positive results would lead to unnecessary and costly NAT testing. While a two-assay strategy may offer marginal cost savings in such scenarios, the group did not find the number of false-positive diagnoses significant enough to justify this approach. The risks associated with false-positive HCV antibody results are minimal, as all individuals diagnosed with HCV exposure require supplemental testing to confirm viremia before initiating antiviral treatment. The recommendations for using RDTs or EIAs/CLIAs/ECLs were based on the assumption that all HCV antibody assays should meet minimum performance criteria, such as WHO prequalification or stringent regulatory review. All in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) should be used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RDTs are preferred in point-of-care settings due to their simplicity and lower infrastructure requirements compared to EIAs, which necessitate additional laboratory equipment and expertise. However, using a second RDT assay would significantly increase costs. A survey of hepatitis testing programs in 19 lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) found that a one-assay serological testing strategy, primarily using RDTs, was being implemented in various hospital-based services, including blood donor screening, harm-reduction services, and HIV treatment clinics. The most sensitive assay available, whether RDT or EIA, should be used to ensure both analytical and clinical sensitivity. RDTs generally have lower analytical sensitivity compared to EIAs, but the chosen assay should minimize false-positive rates. Access to a range of well-performing, quality-assured assays is critical for the success of hepatitis testing programs. While many EIAs are commercially available, there is a lack of HBsAg RDTs that meet minimum performance, safety, and quality standards. National regulatory authorities are responsible for approving RDTs for sale and use after assessing their quality, safety, and performance. All hepatitis B and C testing should follow the manufacturer’s instructions, including an HBsAg neutralization step if applicable. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) and job aids can help minimize testing and reporting errors, improving result quality. Testing environments should adhere to quality management systems and have access to trained, proficient, and motivated laboratory staff. Health-care workers should understand the strengths and limitations of testing strategies, counsel patients appropriately, and act on both positive and negative results. Linkage to care is essential, especially for individuals with false-positive preliminary results, requiring additional testing and clinical evaluation. Retesting strategies should be implemented for those at high risk of acquiring HCV. Ideally, NAT or HCV core antigen testing should be available at the same site as serological testing to enable rapid turnaround, reduce loss to follow-up, and minimize costs associated with referrals to distant centers. Research gaps include evaluating the impact of HIV positivity, CD4 count, viral load, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) exposure on the diagnostic performance of RDTs for HBsAg and HCV antibodies. Further studies are needed to assess the diagnostic performance, cost, and cost-effectiveness of one-assay versus two-assay serological testing strategies in diverse settings. Validation of EIAs and RDTs using less invasive sample collection methods, such as oral fluid, capillary whole blood, and dried blood spots, is also recommended. For chronic hepatitis B (CHB) management, the WHO algorithm provides guidance on treatment and monitoring, including recommendations for settings without access to HBV DNA testing. Treatment is prioritized for individuals with CHB and evidence of compensated or decompensated cirrhosis, regardless of ALT levels, HBeAg status, or HBV DNA levels. Treatment is also recommended for adults with CHB, persistent abnormal ALT levels, and high HBV DNA levels (>20,000 IU/mL), particularly those over 30 years of age. Where HBV DNA testing is unavailable, treatment may be considered based on persistently abnormal ALT levels alone. Antiviral therapy is not recommended for individuals without cirrhosis, persistently normal ALT levels, and low HBV DNA levels (<2,000 IU/mL). Continued monitoring is necessary for all individuals with CHB, particularly those who do not currently meet treatment criteria, to determine if therapy may be indicated in the future to prevent progressive liver disease.
